description: Miami team building a bilingual (English and Spanish) story experience about the robots and instruments NASA left on the Moon and Mars, built on real NASA mission data. Open to a storyteller, illustrator or space science fan who wants to join.
summary:
When Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin left the Moon in 1969, only the top half of their lander flew home. The bottom half is still sitting there, right where they left it. NASA has left machines like it all over the Moon and Mars. Each one did its job, then went quiet.

Ghost Signal is a browser game that lets kids and families call them back.

You pick one of 11 machines on a real NASA map and send it a signal from Earth. The game makes you wait the real time that signal takes to arrive, calculated live from NASA's JPL data. Then the machine answers, in a crackly radio voice from its era. It has forgotten part of its own story, and it needs you to help it remember.

To do that, you open real NASA documents one at a time. Each has one important word blacked out, and the only way to reveal it is to ask the machine the right question, out loud or by typing. Piece its story back together and the machine comes back to life.

Every fact links to its NASA source. It plays in English and Spanish, on any phone or laptop.
details:
The idea. Our challenge was "Abandoned but not Forgotten." Most people have never heard of the machines NASA left behind, and a list of facts won't change that. So we turned each machine into a character you talk to. You don't read about Apollo 11's lander. You call it, and it asks you why it was left behind.

What playing it is like. You start on real NASA maps of the Moon and Mars, built from Moon Trek and Mars Trek images, with each machine at its actual landing site. Tap one and you send a signal from Earth. The wait is real: the game pulls the current distance from NASA JPL Horizons, so a call to the Moon takes about a second. A call to Mars really takes minutes each way; the game shows that number, then lets you skip the wait. The machine's picture builds in through static, its lights come on, and it starts talking.

It remembers some things and not others. You open NASA documents about it one by one. In each, one key word is blacked out. Ask the machine a good question ("Who flew with you?") and the word appears. Collect them all and you rebuild the true sentence, for example: "My bottom half was the launch pad Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin lifted off from." Solve it and the machine comes back in full colour and plays its real recorded words or radio audio.

Why kids remember it. Nobody hands them the answer. They have to ask for it, and something you had to work for sticks. The AI that voices each machine can only use facts we pulled from cited NASA pages, and while you're solving, it is not shown the answer, so it can't give it away or make one up. Every fact shows a link to the NASA page it came from.

Who it's for. It's built for Miami families, so everything works in English and Spanish. It runs in any web browser on a phone or laptop, with nothing to install.

The 11 machines. Eagle (Apollo 11), Surveyor 3, the Apollo science stations left on the Moon, the Apollo 16 Moon buggy, Opportunity, Spirit, Sojourner, Viking 1, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity.

How we built it. JavaScript, HTML and CSS, hosted on GitHub Pages, plus a small server for the voices. ElevenLabs makes the voices and music, OpenAI powers the conversations and understands what players say, and AI image tools helped paint the scenes. Every AI-made image, voice and piece of music is labelled in the game and in the code repository. The facts are not AI-made: each one comes from NASA. Code: https://github.com/absentdsaga/ghost-signal-miami
